one_liner: C++20 secp256k1 ECDSA/Schnorr engine: about 1.5x faster CT signing and 1.1x faster verify than libsecp256k1, and 11-22x faster than OpenSSL.
what_it_does: A secp256k1 library covering ECDSA (RFC 6979, low-S, DER, recovery), BIP-340 Schnorr and ECDH, plus MuSig2, FROST, BIP-32 and BIP-352, with CPU, CUDA/OpenCL/Metal, WASM and ESP32/STM32 backends. It has three API surfaces. The native C++ API has `secp256k1::fast::` (variable-time) and `secp256k1::ct::` (constant-time) namespaces, and the caller picks one at each call site. The `ufsecp_*` C ABI is context-based, has been stable since v3.4.0, and routes every secret-key operation through the CT layer. An opt-in libsecp256k1-compatible shim provides `secp256k1.h` and the module headers so you can swap libraries at link time. It is not an OpenSSL EC API replacement.
how_it_is_fast: Field elements use 5x52-bit limbs (FE52, needs __int128), with optional x86-64 BMI2/ADX assembly and safegcd (Bernstein-Yang) inversion. Verification uses a Strauss/Shamir dual multiplication: GLV endomorphism split plus wNAF, precomputed w=15 odd-multiple tables for G and 2^128*G (8192 entries each, built on the first verify), and an effective-affine (isomorphic-curve) w=5 table for the public key. Constant-time signing uses a libsecp-style signed-digit multi-comb for k*G (11 blocks x 32 entries, Hamburg encoding) with AVX2-vectorized constant-time table scans. The variable-time k*G path uses a large windowed fixed-base table.
when_to_use: Signing-heavy x86-64 services (wallet signers, Taproot key-path and script-path signing) where roughly 1.5x lower CT sign latency than libsecp256k1 matters and you can build with LTO. bench_bitcoin shows +10% on SignTransaction and +35% on SignSchnorrWithMerkleRoot.
Code that currently does secp256k1 ECDSA through OpenSSL's generic EC code (ECDSA_do_sign/ECDSA_do_verify): about 11x faster verify and 22x faster sign, with no OpenSSL dependency.

Projects that need many secp256k1 protocols in one library (MuSig2, FROST, BIP-352 Silent Payments scanning, Ethereum ecrecover, BIP-32), optionally with GPU batch verify or scanning. Sparrow's Frigate uses it for Silent Payments scanning.
Polyglot stacks that want one engine behind the C ABI through its Python, Node.js, Rust, Go, C#, Java or Swift bindings.
Differential testing or evaluation of an alternative backend for code written against libsecp256k1, using the link-time shim.
when_not_to_use: Consensus-critical block validation. The real bench_bitcoin ConnectBlock gain is only +0.9-1.5% with LTO and 0.5-1.0% slower without LTO. Bitcoin Core closed the backend PR (#35469) with a Concept NACK because it lacked human review.

Anywhere that requires an independent security audit. None exists, all audit evidence is self-generated, and serious correctness bugs were fixed as recently as September 2026: Schnorr batch verify accepted invalid signatures (#400), FieldElement::sqrt was wrong for about 18% of inputs (#402), and Pippenger MSM returned wrong points (#401).

Memory- or startup-constrained processes that use the variable-time k*G path. By default it builds a window_bits=18 fixed-base table of about 250 MB (about 5 s of arithmetic) on first use and caches it to a per-user cache directory. Bitcoin Core backend mode uses a compiled-in w=8 table instead.
Browser/WASM, where the README calls CT evidence incomplete, and iOS builds via SPM or CocoaPods, which have CT guards disabled.

Protocols that need libsecp256k1-identical ECDSA nonces with ndata, or custom noncefp callbacks. The shim rejects custom noncefp, and its nonce bytes differ unless you build with SECP256K1_SHIM_RFC6979_COMPAT=ON.

integration.form: static lib (CMake-built libfastsecp256k1; optional libufsecp C ABI library and a libsecp256k1-compatible shim target)
integration.dependencies: None for the CPU build (no Boost or OpenSSL). The GPU backends need the CUDA toolkit, an OpenCL runtime or the Metal SDK. OpenSSL is used only by the benchmark.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 and CMake 3.18+. The README says GCC 11+, Clang 15+ or MSVC 2022. The FAQ says GCC 10+ or Clang 14+, and the shim README says GCC 13+ or Clang 16+.
integration.platforms: x86-64 (the optional asm needs BMI2/ADX; AVX2 is used for CT lookups when available), ARM64, RISC-V RV64GC, Android, iOS, WASM (experimental), ESP32 and STM32. GPU: CUDA 12+, OpenCL, Metal. ROCm/HIP is not validated.
integration.thread_safety: CPU functions are stateless and re-entrant. Global generator tables are built once (call_once, or a mutex-guarded shared_ptr snapshot) and then only read. A ufsecp context or GPU context must not be shared across threads. The shim applies context_randomize blinding per thread, not per context.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the shim can replace libsecp256k1 at link time with no source changes, but it rejects custom noncefp, produces different nonce bytes when ndata is used (unless built with the compat flag), keeps blinding per thread, and holds MuSig2 keyagg state in a process-global map. There is no drop-in path for OpenSSL's EC API.

gotchas: `secp256k1::ecdsa_sign()` in the fast namespace is variable-time: it has data-dependent branches in scalar reduction and the source says not to use it with real keys. Production signing must call `ct::ecdsa_sign` (the C ABI and shim already do). The 21.56x OpenSSL 'FAST' sign ratio was measured on this unsafe path; the CT ratio is 21.70x.

The first variable-time k*G call can take seconds and write a file of about 250 MB (cache_w18.bin) under ~/.cache/secp256k1, ~/Library/Caches or %LOCALAPPDATA%. Set SECP256K1_FIXED_BASE_DISK_CACHE=OFF to prevent this. The precompute path can throw std::runtime_error.

The speedups depend on LTO and a locked CPU frequency. Without LTO, ConnectBlock is slower. In an unlocked-frequency run, libsecp256k1 was 7.5% faster on ConnectBlockAllEcdsa; the repo calls that result a measurement artifact.

The docs contradict each other. For example, the shim README still shows CT ECDSA sign 9% slower than libsecp256k1 and cites 'OpenSSL 3.x', while the canonical benchmark shows 1.52x faster and does not record the OpenSSL version. The verify tables (about 1.3 MB) stay allocated at exit and trigger leak checkers unless you call release_process_resources().
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the siblings is an alternative for the same curve. ENG25519 does X25519/Ed25519, fasthqc is the HQC KEM and VecFalcon is Falcon signing. Pick this one only when the protocol requires secp256k1 ECDSA or BIP-340 Schnorr, as Bitcoin and Ethereum do.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own bench_unified was run with GCC 14.2.0 Release+LTO (-O3 -march=native) on an i5-14400F with turbo off and a pinned core, taking the median of 11 passes. CT ECDSA sign took 19.3 us, versus 29.4 us for an in-tree libsecp256k1 snapshot (f9a944f, compiled without LTO) and 419 us for system OpenSSL ECDSA_do_sign (version not recorded). ECDSA verify took 36.8 us, versus 41.5 us and 400 us. Bitcoin Core's bench_bitcoin ConnectBlock shrinks the advantage to +0.9-1.5% with LTO.
status_note: Actively developed: v4.6.0 was released 2026-09-24 and the dev branch has commits through 2026-09-26. It is MIT-licensed and ships as CMake builds plus apt, brew, pip, npm and NuGet packages. Adoption is thin (55 stars, one publicly known production adopter) and there is no third-party audit.
